konular: Limits of SFT and preference data

sorular.soru: A team uses GRPO with an automatic answer checker to raise a model's math scores. Which goal does this training mainly serve?
secenekler: Capability: getting answers right when they can be checked, as in math or code
Harmlessness: avoiding answers that could hurt people or help with dangerous tasks
Honesty: making the model say clearly when it is not sure about its answer
Tone and format: making answers sound friendly and look the way users expect
sorular.aciklama: A checker rewards correct answers, so this training mainly builds capability rather than alignment. Harmlessness and honesty are alignment goals, taught mostly with human preferences as in RLHF or DPO, and a math checker cannot judge them.

sorular.konu: Limits of SFT and preference data
sorular.soru: Two answers to a beginner's question are both correct, but one is much easier to follow. What does preference learning teach here that SFT alone does not?
secenekler: How to write a correct answer by copying one expert example word by word
How to choose which of several correct answers fits the user better
How to check if an answer is right by using a fixed automatic rule
How to answer new topics by adding more facts to what the model already knows
sorular.aciklama: SFT shows the model what one good answer looks like, while preference learning compares answers and teaches which one fits the user better. Copying an expert example is what SFT already does, so it adds nothing new here.

sorular.konu: Limits of SFT and preference data
sorular.soru: Why is asking people 'Which of these two answers is better?' often more reliable than asking them to score each answer from one to five?
secenekler: Comparing two answers removes labeler bias, such as a liking for long answers
Scores from one to five cannot be turned into training data for a reward model
A choice between two answers gives a reward number that RL can use directly
People use score scales differently, but agree more on which one is better
sorular.aciklama: One person's four can be another person's three, so scores are hard to compare, while picking the better of two answers is quick and more consistent. Pairs do not remove bias, because labelers can still prefer longer or more confident answers.

sorular.soru: In standard RLHF, which order of steps is correct?
secenekler: First update the policy with RL, then train a reward model on its new answers
First train a reward model on comparisons, then use RL to update the policy
Train the reward model and the policy at the same time with one shared loss
First train a reward model, then use it only to pick answers at use time
sorular.aciklama: RLHF first turns human comparisons into a reward model, and then RL uses its scores to update the policy, which is the LLM itself. Using a reward model only to pick the best answer at use time is Best-of-N, which skips RL.

sorular.soru: Why does RLHF train a reward model instead of asking people to score each new answer during RL?
secenekler: RL needs scores for a huge number of new answers, and people are too slow
People cannot compare two answers well, so a model must make every choice
The reward model writes better answers than people, so it replaces SFT data
The reward model keeps the policy close to the SFT model during training
sorular.aciklama: RL makes a huge number of fresh answers, so a reward model learns from human comparisons and then scores those answers in place of people. Keeping the policy close to the SFT model is the job of the KL penalty, not of the reward model.

sorular.soru: When RL is used to train a language model, what counts as one action of the agent?
secenekler: Giving a score to the full answer after the answer is finished
Changing the model weights after each batch of training data
Choosing the next token, based on the prompt and the text so far
Choosing which prompt from the dataset the model should answer next
sorular.aciklama: The agent is the language model, the state is the prompt plus the text so far, and each action is the next token. Scoring the finished answer is the reward step, done by a reward model or a checker, so it is not an action of the agent.

sorular.soru: During RLHF, a team makes the KL penalty very strong. What will most likely happen?
secenekler: The policy moves far from the SFT model and learns to fool the reward model
The reward model is updated more often, so its scores become more accurate
The policy gets the best results, because all reward hacking is now blocked
The policy stays close to the SFT model and learns little from the reward
sorular.aciklama: The KL penalty charges the policy for moving away from the SFT model, so with a very strong penalty the safest choice is to barely change. It does lower the risk of reward hacking, but it also blocks the useful changes that the reward asks for.

sorular.soru: In PPO training of a language model, what is the job of the critic, also called the value model?
secenekler: It scores each finished answer, based on what humans liked in comparisons
It predicts the expected reward, so each real reward can be compared with it
It is a frozen SFT copy that shows how far the policy has moved from the start
It writes fresh answers to the prompts, so PPO always has new data to learn from
sorular.aciklama: The critic predicts how much reward to expect, and the advantage compares the real reward with this guess. Scoring finished answers by human taste is the job of the reward model, a separate model that stays frozen during PPO.

sorular.soru: PPO clipping and the KL penalty both limit how much the policy changes. How are their jobs different?
secenekler: Clipping keeps the whole training near the SFT model, while KL limits each update step
Clipping limits the reward model's scores, while KL limits the critic's value guesses
Clipping limits each update step, while KL keeps the whole training near the SFT model
Clipping stops answers from getting too long, while KL stops the model from refusing
sorular.aciklama: Clipping compares the policy with the recent copy that made the rollouts, so one update cannot jump too far. The KL penalty compares it with the frozen SFT model, so it is KL, not clipping, that keeps the whole training near the start.

sorular.soru: What is the main practical benefit of DPO over RLHF with PPO?
secenekler: It learns straight from stored pairs, with no reward model and no RL loop
It learns without any preference data, from one target answer for each prompt
It learns without a reference model, so only one model must be kept in memory
It learns from single thumbs-up or thumbs-down labels instead of answer pairs
sorular.aciklama: DPO turns preference pairs into a direct loss on the policy, so it skips the separate reward model and the PPO loop. It still keeps a frozen reference model, and learning from single yes or no labels is the idea behind KTO.

sorular.soru: DPO has no separate reward model, yet it still keeps a frozen reference model. What is the reference model for?
secenekler: It writes new answer pairs during training, because DPO needs fresh rollouts
It decides which answer in each pair is better, in place of the human labelers
It is trained together with the policy, so both models learn the same preferences
It is a fixed starting point that pulls the policy back if it moves too far
sorular.aciklama: DPO measures each answer by how much the policy has changed its probability compared with the reference, and this pull keeps the policy near its start, like the KL penalty in RLHF. The answer pairs come from stored data, so the reference does not write new ones.

sorular.soru: A teacher marks each student's answer as better or worse than the class average. Which method judges a model's answers in the same way?
secenekler: PPO, which asks a trained critic model to guess how good each answer will be
GRPO, which compares each answer with the other answers to the same prompt
Best-of-N, which keeps only the top-scored answer and throws the rest away
DPO, which compares one chosen answer with one rejected answer from stored data
sorular.aciklama: GRPO samples a group of answers for one prompt and uses the group's average reward as the baseline, just like a class average. PPO gets its baseline from a separate critic model, which is the part GRPO removes.

sorular.soru: A team wants to use GRPO for a chatbot that writes friendly emails, but no automatic checker can mark an email right or wrong. Can GRPO still be used?
secenekler: Yes, because GRPO can take its rewards from a learned reward model instead
No, because GRPO needs a rule that can mark each answer right or wrong
No, because GRPO needs a critic model, and a critic learns only from checkers
Yes, but people must score every sampled answer by hand during training
sorular.aciklama: The reward source and the update method are separate choices, so GRPO can use a checker or a learned reward model. Checkers are popular with GRPO for math and code, but they are one option, not a requirement.

sorular.soru: An AI judge that labels answer pairs tends to prefer the longer answer. Its labels then train a reward model for RL. What will most likely happen?
secenekler: The bias goes away, because the judge uses the same written rules every time
The reward model ignores length, because it only looks at the gap in scores
The policy is not affected, because it sees reward scores and not labels
The policy learns to write longer answers, because the bias is passed on
sorular.aciklama: RLAIF copies the judge's biases into the labels, so the reward model learns to like length and the policy follows it. Using the same rules every time makes labels consistent, but a consistent bias is still a bias.

sorular.soru: In Constitutional AI, which part of the work do humans still do?
secenekler: They label every answer pair, saying which answer is less harmful
They write the improved answers that the model is fine-tuned on
They write the principles the AI uses to check and judge answers
They give the reward scores that the policy tries to raise during RL
sorular.aciklama: Humans write the constitution, a list of principles, and the AI uses it to check its own answers, rewrite them and judge which answer is less harmful. Labeling every pair by hand is what RLHF does, and Constitutional AI replaces those labels with AI feedback.

sorular.soru: Best-of-N skips RL training. It samples several answers and returns the one with the top reward score. What is the main cost of this approach?
secenekler: Every request needs many answers made and scored, which costs time and money
It needs an answer checker, so it only works for tasks like math and code
A person must pick the best answer for each request while the user waits for it
It must keep a critic and a reference model, so it needs much more memory
sorular.aciklama: Best-of-N leaves the model unchanged and does its work at use time, so every request costs several generations plus scoring. Its scores come from a reward model, so it is not limited to tasks that an answer checker can mark.

sorular.soru: Why does PPO keep sampling fresh answers after a few updates instead of reusing one large set of old answers?
secenekler: The reward model is retrained after each update, so old scores go out of date
The reference model changes after each update, so old KL values become wrong
The policy has changed, so old answers no longer show what it would do now
Stored answers cannot be scored again once the reward model has seen them
sorular.aciklama: PPO is on-policy, so it learns from answers made by the current or a very recent policy. The reward model and the reference stay frozen, so they are not the reason, and reusing old data saves cost but needs extra care.

sorular.soru: After preference tuning, a chatbot follows instructions better and is safer, but it is worse at math than before. What does this show?
secenekler: Reward hacking: the model found a trick to get high scores without real quality
Over-refusal: the model became so careful that it says no to safe requests
A trade-off: alignment improved some behaviors but hurt an old skill
Labeler disagreement: people did not agree on which answers were better
sorular.aciklama: Alignment often improves instruction following and safety but can cost variety or old skills, which is called the alignment tax. Reward hacking means a high score while the true goal is missed, and nothing here shows a trick to raise the score.
